title: Fear: the mark of the excellent and the conduct of the base
claim: The book awards fear and fearlessness to opposite ranks of people. Fearlessness (அஞ்சாமை) is one of the four things a king must never lack (382), yet not fearing what should be feared is folly and fearing it is the work of the knowing (அறிவார் தொழில், 428), and the excellent fear evil deeds that the practised wrongdoer does not (201). At the other end, fear is the whole of the base person's good conduct (அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம், 1075), the only check on a freedom 1073 compares to the gods'. Taken together, the verses make fear itself morally neutral: what ranks a person is its object. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both notice the collision at 428 and resolve it the same way, saying that since fearlessness was called a king's excellence, 428 names the things that must be feared (sin, blame, ruin), while Parimelazhagar reads 1075's fear as fear of the king's punishment.
limits: This does not claim the book has one doctrine of fear; the reconciliation by object is the commentators', and 382 and 1075 do not themselves say what is or is not feared. 201's 'fear' is of a sin-induced intoxication on Parimelazhagar's reading, which is further from 1075 than the shared word suggests.

title: Does a fort cure fear, or does fear cancel a fort?
claim: Three verses in the Book of Wealth tie fortification and fear together in a loop. A fort is of value to those who, afraid, look to their own safety (அஞ்சித் தற்போற்றுபவர்க்கும் பொருள், 741); a king who has made no defence will be seized by fear when war comes and quickly perish (569); yet the fearful have no fort at all (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை, 534). Read together they make the fort necessary but not sufficient: its absence produces fear, but fear in the mind makes it useless, which is how Parimelazhagar reads 534 (forests and hills give no profit to a frightened mind). This also gives the kingly fearlessness of 382 a material condition, since 569 shows even a king coming to fear without preparation.
limits: 534's fort is a simile for the heedless losing their wealth, so its first half is not primarily a claim about statecraft; and 741's 'afraid' is, on Parimelazhagar's reading, the weaker party prudently taking refuge, not the cowardice 534 condemns. The loop is a reader's construction across chapters 54, 57 and 75, not something any verse states.

title: Bowing: good for all, yet shameful in some
claim: The book commends பணிதல் without restriction in three places: bowing is good for everyone and a further wealth for the rich (125), whoever wants a lineage must be humble toward all (யார்க்கும் பணிவு, 960), and greatness always bows while smallness admires itself (978). Other verses then draw lines the general rule does not. 963 makes bowing the duty of abundance and standing tall the duty of want; 903 names a bowing that brings lasting shame, stooping before one's wife; and the honour chapter prefers being called ruined to living by following those who slight you (967), while 680 reports that rulers of small domains do bow to the great and take terms. Read together, the praised humility is the absence of pride in those who could be proud (Parimelazhagar glosses 125 and 978 by பெருமிதம் and தருக்கு), and bowing from fear or for a living is a different act the book does not praise: Parimelazhagar says of 680 that bowing is not the wish of the honourable, so the verse says 'they will accept' as worldly practice.
limits: The unifying distinction between humility and submission is the commentators' more than the text's; Parimelazhagar reads 978's என்றும் as 'even when distinction has come', which removes its tension with 963, and Manakkudavar takes 680 as plain prescription for the weak, not a reluctant report. 963's 'reduced circumstances' is poverty on both commentators' readings, so its clash with 680 holds only if personal honour extends to statecraft.
